The GVWG 2007 Annual General Meeting is coming. See page 2 for details.
If you missed our January meeting you missed
(as Mr Sullivan would say) “A Really Big
Shoo”. I counted over 90 people and more
came in after I was done. What a terrific
event. Our outstanding attendance probably
had a lot to do with the excellent calibre of
our presenters. Bill Smith of Mt Vernon,
Washington demonstrated how he does a
barley twist on a goblet stem (which he donated to our annual auction) and then our
own Art Liestman shared a wealth of information about equipment and techniques of
pyrography. Thanks to you both for your
excellent presentations.
During the meeting this month we will hold
our Annual General Meeting. There will be
two executive seats up for election – Vice
President and Treasurer as well as two seats
for members-at-large. We will also present a
financial report and other required items for
an AGM. Please attend and contribute to the
meeting. In advance, I would like to thank
Steve Hansen who is finishing his term as VP
and to Merv Graham who has served the
maximum term (4 years) as our Treasurer.
Thanks very much for your service to the
Guild, guys. It is only though their kind of
volunteerism that the Guild prospers.
We have two world-class turners here in
March. Eli Avisera will be here on Sunday
March 4th for a day-long demonstration and
classes on Thursday March 1 and possibly
also on Friday, March 2. Those who saw Eli
last year were very impressed with his skill
and inventive style. We are fortunate to have
arranged a large demonstration space on the
SFU campus on Burnaby Mountain. We will
be mailing out directions closer to the day so
watch for them and plan to attend.
Later in March we have a day-long demo at
Sapperton (Saturday) and two 1-day (Sunday
and Monday) classes with Nick Cook. Nick is
a production turner in the Atlanta area and
has lots of stories to tell while he churns out
projects non-stop. If you want to improve
your skills or become faster at what you do
then this is a demo not to be missed. By

He then removes the tailstock, drills
the bowl and hollows it, using a Oneway Termite ring tool. Sand and finish
the inside of the bowl next, true the
rim, and finish it. Bill likes Hut Crystal
Coat. Bring the tailstock back, using a
cone attachment covered with tape to
prevent burnishing. Finish the bowl of
the goblet, make a bead at the base,
and start removing wood to form the
stem. Remove the wood in sections,
working back towards the base. Shape
the base, and put another bead at the
junction of the stem. Use the skew to
size and smooth the stem, then sand it
smooth. This is not the place to say
“good enough” – do it right.

Bill Smith came up from Mount
Vernon to show us that turning a barley twist is not as complicated or time
consuming as it seems. The number of
tools required is also fairly
limited. The specialized
tools Bill uses are a flexible
rasp file and a chain saw file
with the end cut off to allow
him to file right to the end.
Other than that, the tools
are ones that we already
have.
Bill starts with 2 ¼” x 9”
stock. Straight grained hardwood is best. He uses a
3/8” spindle gouge or skew
to round his stock then
mounts it in a chuck, bringing up the tailstock for stability. He shapes the bowl of

Thanks to the arm-twisting ability of
our speaker committee (The Gang of
Three), our own Art Liestman was
convinced to share his knowledge on
pyrography with us. Art has used pyrography on his pieces for a long time,
from his burning fields works to his
current puzzle illusion works. In his
current work, burned lines help to
define shapes and prevent colour
bleeding.
As usual, Art has all the cool (hot??)
tools, and was able to point us in the
right direction if we choose to go that
way. That said, lots of cool tools are
not essential. Burned lines can be created using the lathe and a piece of
sharpened linoleum or very coarse
sandpaper. For more extensive burning, a base unit and pens are needed.

Set up your work space so that you
are relaxed and comfortable. Use a
fan or carving dust unit to remove
smoke. Apparently, the best fans are
purple. Practice makes perfect, and
curves burn differently than a flat surface, so practice on your roughed out
bowls. Different woods burn differently too, with soft woods burning
faster than hard woods. Wood like
ash is a poor choice, as lines will be
blotchy. Maple is a good choice.
Finish is applied after burning. Sanding
with 320 grit will remove scorch
marks. Deep burns can be covered
with ink to enhance them.
A final pointer for a successful piece is
that surface decoration will not improve an ugly piece. Plan the piece so
it is enhanced by the decoration – do
not decide at the end to try to add on
in an effort to improve it.
As usual, Art was as entertaining as he
was informative. Thanks for sharing
your knowledge, Art.
finger-guard helps to anchor the piece

To draw lines, use a tip shaped like a
skew. It needs to be sharpened so it
cuts. Use a stone once, then keep the
tip sharp with frequent use of a hone
or leather strop. Use a longer blade
for straight lines, a shorter one for
curves. The technique is to put the tip
in, roll onto the blade and pull along,
keeping the blade in the groove. In
order to avoid a heavier line at the
start, you have to get the tip in and
move quickly, then slow down. All of
this is easier if you keep your hand
anchored on the piece.
Use a pointillism tip for dots. A
hooked tool allows you to either do
shading, deep burning, or hatch marks
by holding it on its side. A sharpened
#6 tip is the best tip for signing your
work, but it still is not easy. Remember that when you change tips, you will
need to tweak the temperature. Always test on a piece of scrap wood.
Brands can be used too, but they need
a high powered base unit. Molly Winton sells spheres and squares. Razor

Richard Raffan has been a major influence on a generation of woodturners
worldwide, both technically and artistically. His books, Turning Wood, Turned
Bowl Design, Turning Boxes, Turning
Bowls and Taunton’s Complete Illustrated
Guide to Turning are woodturning classics. Tens of thousands of woodturners learned the craft from Raffan videos and DVDs.
Since 1980 Richard Raffan has taught in
a dozen countries across North America, Europe and Australasia. Now
semi-retired, he limits his teaching to
just a few weeks each year, but still
creates work for exhibitions and on
commission.

Richard Raffan
Richard Raffan began turning wood in
England in 1970 at the age of 26, after
a successful career in the London wine
trade. He has earned his living as a
woodturner ever since, and emigrated
to Australia in 1982.
After five months working in a traditional woodturning workshop, Richard
Raffan set up on his own. Working in
isolation, he turned “one-off” bowls,
platters, boxes, and scoops, and for
these he had to create a market
amongst the craft galleries that were
beginning to appear.
In 1973 Richard Raffan was the only
woodturner represented in the seminal exhibition The Craftsmans Art at the
V & A Museum in London. This quickly

leave with you, and I am sure Claudia
and Art will agree, is the fact that
these symposia have all kinds of valuable information for beginners as well
as more experienced turners. If you
think this a huge plug for our visiting
demonstrators and our Symposium,
you are right.
Like our Symposium in September, the
Arizona woodturners had a world
class group of demonstrators covering
a broad section of the craft and art. In
my mind, the best of the bunch was
our own past president, Art Liestman.
Art dealt with problems in form before he went on to surface enhancement. Binh Pho, Tony Cortese, Trent
Bosch, and Robert Rosand covered
different aspects of the subject.

Eli Avisera, from Jerusalem, Israel, will
be here for hands-on classes on
Thursday and Friday, March 1st and 2nd
and for a lecture/demo on Sunday,
March 4th. Those of you who managed to see Eli last year will be anxious
to see him again, and those of you
who missed him then get a second
chance.
Eli graduated from the school of wood
art in Jerusalem, his home town. In
1988, Eli established the "Wood Craft
Center" in Jerusalem where he
teaches workshops for furniture building, wood turning and wood carving at
all skill levels.
Eli’s creations are exhibited in many
exhibitions around the world. He has
been invited to many countries to
show his unique variety of techniques.
Eli uses a line of his own signature
tools (manufactured by Hamlet Tools
UK). These unique tools have been
developed based on over 30 years of
experience in woodturning.
If you’d like to know more about Eli,
please see his website at http://
avisera.co.il/.

The Bellevue Arts Museum is presenting
Turning Wood into Art: The Jane and Arthur Mason Collection, 120 works by more
than 40 artists from the collection of Jane
and Arthur Mason. This exhibition was organized by the Mint Museum of Craft + Design and represents one of the most significant assembling of contemporary turned
wood objects in America today. The exhibition runs until April 8, 2007. The museum
is located at 510 Bellevue Way. More information is at http://www.bellevueart.org/
